newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's "Dirty Harry" suffers blow in drugs war.
newsitem.headline: Manila's "Dirty Harry" suffers blow in drugs war.

text.p: The Philippines' top anti-drugs crusader was ordered on Thursday to stop branding the homes of suspected drug pushers with "Get out" signs after lawyers said he was behaving like Adolf Hitler.

Judge Librado Correa directed Manila's mayor Alfredo Lim to suspend his anti-drugs campaign for 20 days so the court could study the petition by a lawyers group which wants the campaign permanently banned.
The group said even drug pushers had rights and likened Lim's methods to Hitler's campaign of branding the homes of Jews with the Star of David.
"He has become an accuser, judge and executioner at the same time," lawyer Leonard de Vera said.
Lim said he would bow to the judge's order.
"This is a sad day for law enforcers but a happy day for drug pushers," he said.

But the feisty former policeman, dubbed the "Dirty Harry" of the Philippines -- after the trigger-happy Hollywood detective played by actor Clint Eastwood -- for his iron-fisted handling of criminals, added:
"I want the drug pushers not to make this ruling a cause for celebration. We have other ways of penalising them. The fight is not yet over."
In his unorthodox campaign, Lim leads vice squads in smearing the doors of suspects with signs in red paint reading "A pusher lives here, get out" or "Drug protector. Beat it!".
Since launching his war on July 1, the former policeman has branded nearly 300 houses with such signs, and driven 60 percent of their occupants out of the city, he said.
In 1992, he endeared himself to the Roman Catholic church by shutting down Manila's "red light" district, throwing thousands of prostitutes out of work.
Lim has defended his "scarlet letter" campaign, saying legal loopholes allow pushers to easily post bail and continue with their activities.
President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday drug trafficking had become "a national security threat."
Tough anti-drug laws prescribe death for anyone carrying at least 200 grams of methamphetamine crystals, called "ice", or least 40 grams of cocaine or heroin.
But the drug menace has grown, with 1.6 million Filipinos now using "ice," officials said. Efforts to curb the problem have failed because syndicates are protected by policemen, they said.
